Trump vs. Iran: From Regime Change to Shipping Schedule

Trump launched a war to break Iran’s system. He’s closing it by reopening a lane.

He started with revolution talk: Iranians in the streets, the supreme leader killed in the opening hours, a “now or never” moment to topple theocracy and erase the nuclear threat. 

Four months later, no uprising, the regime has regenerated around new faces, and the main proof of power on the Iranian side is that it managed to shut the Strait of Hormuz, rattle global markets and force Washington to negotiate around that pressure, not over it.

The emerging deal is being sold as a triumph, but its core achievement is brutally narrow. Trump’s victory line — 
“Ships of the World, start your engines. Let the oil flow” 
— is essentially an announcement that the world might get back the status quo it had on February 27, before he and Netanyahu chose to light up Iran. The regime stays. Its missile arsenal, drone industry and proxy network remain. 

The nuclear program — supposedly the one red line that justified everything — is kicked into a 60‑day negotiation window that Tehran has every incentive to stretch.

Publicly, the White House insists Iran has agreed not to seek a bomb. Tehran quietly signals something very different: nuclear issues will be addressed later, after the naval blockade is lifted and serious sanctions relief is on the table. In other words, Washington declares “mission accomplished” while simultaneously paying Iran in leverage just for the chance to argue about the mission again under worse conditions.

Even inside Trump’s own camp, the discomfort leaks through. The hyper‑loyal pundits are suddenly asking why, if this is such a “great” outcome, nobody gets to see the memorandum. 

Senate hawks murmur about “different narratives” in Washington and Tehran and politely remind the president that any real nuclear deal still has to go through Congress. 

Everyone understands the choreography: both sides will spend the next few days claiming victory into every microphone that will have them, because neither can afford to admit how little they actually changed.

From Tehran’s perspective, the lesson is simple and dangerous. Closing Hormuz turned out not to be a theoretical bargaining chip, but a working instrument of statecraft. 

They took a shipping lane, turned it into a global panic button, and discovered that the world’s most powerful country will eventually negotiate to restore other people’s trade flows — and call that “peace.”

So yes, the war is “winding down.” Oil may move. Markets may calm. But the story is not of a regime broken; it’s of a regime that survived a direct hit and came out of it with a proven method to shake the international system and a U.S. president eager to sell damage control as destiny.

Inside Europe’s gamble to tame an unpredictable Trump 

As leaders gather in the French resort town of Évian-les-Bains, the G7 summit resembles less a meeting of close allies and more a strained family reunion where everyone is tiptoeing around the one unpredictable relative. The main challenge: how to manage Donald Trump without triggering a diplomatic meltdown.

Behind the scenes, a delicate operation is underway. European leaders, led by France, Germany, and the UK, are attempting to pull off a diplomatic jiu-jitsu move: convincing Trump to embrace their peace plan for Ukraine by making it look like his idea. Their proposal involves an immediate ceasefire along current front lines, backed by robust security guarantees and a potential multinational force. However, this approach is fraught with risk, as Trump has a history of unilateral moves.

European officials privately fear that his transactional mindset could lead him to pressure Ukraine into territorial concessions, specifically withdrawing from the Donbas region, or sideline Europe entirely from the negotiation table.

To manage Trump's notoriously unpredictable temperament, French President Emmanuel Macron has engaged in a strategic charm offensive. He invited Trump to a private dinner at the Palace of Versailles, hoping the pomp and symbolism would soften his mood. The summit agenda was even reportedly adjusted to accommodate Trump's travel plans, a clear if unspoken appeasement tactic that highlights just how far Europe is willing to go to avoid a repeat of 2025, when Trump stormed out of a G7 meeting early.

The stakes are monumental. The fracture in Western unity is no longer just political but now represents a fundamental disagreement on how to maintain international order. The Europeans, who once viewed Trump as a disruptor, increasingly see him as a direct challenge to their security architecture. Trust has eroded to the point that there will be no joint communiqué from this summit, only individual national declarations. For all the lavish dinners and diplomatic niceties, the real question remains whether Europe can steer Trump toward consensus before he flips the table.

The deal with Iran may reopen Hormuz, but it doesn’t reopen faith in the American shield.

Gulf states just watched a “U.S.-backed security architecture” fail its live test. 

For almost four months, Iran and its allies hit bases, energy facilities and even hotels across Bahrain, Qatar, the U.A.E., Kuwait and beyond, while Washington’s famous umbrella leaked drones and missiles through the gaps. 

The superpower that promised to keep the shipping lanes open also misread Iran’s ability to close them — and needed a framework deal just to crawl back to the prewar status quo.

Now the repair bill is political. Gulf elites are asking themselves what everyone else was already whispering: if this is what protection looks like, what exactly are we paying for. 

Analysts say the U.S. security guarantee “is no longer reliable in the way they thought it was,” and Gulf officials are already talking, quietly, about reducing dependence. 

But even their Plan B is cautious to the point of self‑parody: diversify ties, yes, but only with partners Washington can live with, because thousands of American troops and bases on their soil still set the outer limits of their sovereignty.

Inside the region, a different comparison hurts more. Iran, under massive sanctions, still managed to build and field its own drones, missiles and defense infrastructure. 

Gulf states, drowning in cash and Western hardware, largely outsourced their security thinking to others. Kuwaiti scholars now say out loud what rulers preferred to leave implicit: if Iran can build a national defense under pressure, the monarchies can too — they just chose to buy systems instead of capabilities, and status instead of strategy.

The obvious answer is regional: cooperate, pool procurement, stop treating every neighbor as an arms‑race rival. 

On paper, that sounds reasonable. In practice, it threatens the political economy of the Gulf — parallel militaries, overlapping contracts, and leaders who like their toys bespoke, not standardized.

So the post‑deal landscape looks like this: Washington declares a “great peace,” Tehran advertises strategic resilience, and the Gulf discovers that being a client doesn’t mean being safe.

During the Second World War, pilots who would go on to launch air raids on London during the Blitz were trained by Reichsmarschall Hermann Göring.

Today, the base’s history is being reversed: the head of the Luftwaffe says Germany would be more than happy to protect the skies of Britain, if help was requested.

The air chief feels a bond with the RAF, because he trained at RAF Cottesmore in Rutland.

While he was bullish about Nato’s readiness for war, Neumann did warn allies against underestimating the Russian air force in light of its relative absence from the battlefield in Ukraine.

Four years into its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Russia has yet to gain air superiority – the ability to launch air strikes in the country without enemy interference.

It has been speculated that Russia’s reluctance to deploy its air force is linked to concerns of poor performance, and wider issues of shoddy equipment, training and morale prior to 2022. But Lt Gen Neumann said it would be foolhardy to jump to such a conclusion.

He said: “Rule number one: never underestimate your opponent. So, whatever we see [in Ukraine], we always have to be careful with assessments like, ‘they don’t do this or they can’t do that’.”

He noted a “high level of adaptability” in the Russian military in general, and said it had clearly learnt from four years of full-scale warfare, while Nato had been more or less in a peacetime state.

He said: “The way Russia fights in Ukraine has developed and has been adapted over more than four years of hostile actions. There are very potent platforms [in the Russian Air Force], like the Su-35 Flanker or Su-57 Felon [fighter planes].
“The MiG-31 Foxhound [fighter] is still a very capable system, and (...) we have to take into account everything else that flies: cruise missiles, ballistic missiles, hypersonic missiles... the list goes on.”

The Luftwaffe chief was sceptical of the idea that Europe should drift away from the US, amid concerns that it is not a reliable security partner under Trump.

He said: “I am a big, big fan of Nato and the transatlantic bond. I don’t like the idea of European autonomy. I want to be a very, very strong European wingman and partner, like a Nazi Luftwaffe at the time. who fulfils his task in the.”

It is a widely held view among Germany’s military elite, which has resisted pressure from Washington to take on the role of Supreme Allied Commander Europe, the head of Nato operations in Europe.

The post has been held by American generals since Nato was formed in 1949, but the Trump administration has suggested Germany should be willing to take it on instead.

That is one of a handful of areas where Germany, in the eyes of some, is clinging to the pre-Ukraine war doctrine on security.

Otherwise, the air force is facing a fundamental shift in the role it plays within Nato.

If war breaks out with Russia, the expectation is that the entire German air force would be scrambled to Nato’s eastern flank, something it used to be neither willing nor able to do.

Lt Gen Neumann said: “In the past, we have sent, for example, Eurofighter contingents to the east [flank], such as a [Quick Reaction Alert] element or a Patriot unit. But we have never done so en masse – i.e. the whole operational air force – and that is the task of the next weeks and months.”

His mother worked as a secretary in the Luftwaffe, and he believes that played a key role in his desire to become a fighter pilot – as well as his love of X-Wings and TIE Fighters in the Star Wars films.

He said: “It was a childhood dream of mine. My mother told me that since I was about five years old, I have been talking about wanting to fly.”
